analysis.one_liner: Bans lead in toys and other products made for young children.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate committee it was sent to and died when the Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would treat any product marketed to children under age six that contains lead over set limits as a banned hazardous substance. Limits would start at 600 parts per million, drop to 250 after one year, and 100 after two years, with the Consumer Product Safety Commission able and eventually required to push limits lower if feasible. Electronics that cannot meet the limits would need child-resistant covers instead, and stronger state lead laws would stay in force.
analysis.who_benefits: Parents and young children, who would face less lead exposure from toys and other children's products. Lead is a known neurotoxin with no safe level for children, and the 2007 recall wave of lead-tainted toys made in China put this issue in the news.

how_it_helps.text: Bans children's products containing lead above 600 ppm immediately, 250 ppm after one year, and 100 ppm after two years, treating them as banned hazardous substances under federal law [S3].
Directs the Consumer Product Safety Commission to review the standard five years after enactment and set the lowest lead level that is feasible to achieve, and lets it tighten limits sooner [S2][S3].

Requires electronic children's products that cannot meet the limits to have child-resistant coverings limiting access to lead-containing parts, with a compliance schedule the Commission can set [S2][S3].
Leaves in place any state or local lead laws that protect consumers at least as strongly, so states could go further [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Toy makers, importers, and retailers, who would need lead-free materials, testing, and compliance programs. Electronics makers would face some cost too, though the bill gives them a cover-and-casing alternative where meeting the lead limits is not feasible.

drawbacks.text: Reformulating products and testing every component costs money, and the bill gives companies as little as 30 days before the first limit applies, which smaller manufacturers may struggle to meet [S3].
The bill focuses on products for children under six, leaving older children's items uncovered under this definition [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit is substantial: removing lead from products young children mouth and handle prevents irreversible developmental harm, and the bill already built in a phase-in and an electronics exemption to ease industry costs. The compliance burden is real but modest relative to the harm lead exposure causes.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate Commerce Committee and never received any further action before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Barack Obama introduced the bill with six Democratic cosponsors on October 3, 2007 [S1][S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day [S5].
No further action was ever recorded — no hearings, no markup, no committee or floor vote — and the bill died when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Toy and children's product manufacturers avoided new lead limits, testing requirements, and compliance costs that the bill would have imposed. Families with young children went on bearing the risk the bill aimed to remove.

sides.party_line_note: All six cosponsors were Democrats, and no Republican support is recorded; no votes were ever held, so the record shows no opposition votes either [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Toy and children's product manufacturers and importers
industries.note: The bill would have required lead-free materials, component testing, and staged compliance for products for children under six. Its death meant no federal lead limits from this bill and no new testing obligations; the industry's cost interest ran against children's safety.
They would have faced the same lead limits but could keep lead-containing parts behind child-resistant casings where meeting the limits was not feasible, a softer path than full compliance.
